# The Periodic Table

## Core ideas and reasoning

The periodic table arranges elements by increasing proton number. A period corresponds to occupied electron shells in the introductory main-group model, while members of a main group have related valence electron arrangements and chemical behaviour. Group I metals lose one electron to form +1 ions; Group II commonly forms +2 ions. Group VII halogens commonly gain one electron to form -1 ions. Group 0 noble gases have filled outer shells under ordinary conditions and low reactivity; helium has two outer electrons rather than eight. Metallic character is generally found on the left and decreases across a period, while nonmetals occupy the right. Use an element's electron arrangement to infer its position, then explain its likely ion formation. Hydrogen has distinctive chemistry and should not be treated as an ordinary alkali metal. Transition elements occupy the central block and can show variable oxidation states and coloured compounds. Position gives trends, but use actual evidence when comparing specific substances.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

An atom has electron arrangement 2,8,2. State its period and main group in KCSE group notation.

Period 3 because there are three occupied shells; Group II because there are two outer-shell electrons.

### Example 2

Explain why Group I elements commonly form +1 ions.

They lose their single outer electron, leaving a filled underlying shell and one more proton than electrons.

### Example 3

Why are noble gases generally unreactive?

Their outer electron shells are filled, so gaining, losing or sharing electrons is usually energetically unfavourable under ordinary conditions.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
